chunks: PVT impact on power and performance. The question: How does process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) impact power, performance, and thermals?
PVT stands for process, voltage and temperature. The same chip design does not behave identically every time. Manufacturing makes each chip slightly different (process).
The voltage the transistors actually receive is a bit lower than the setting (voltage). The chip also runs hot or cold (temperature). Each of these changes speed, power and heat.
Fast chips tend to waste more power, so designers check the extremes and add safety margin.
Picture a school sports day. Process is the runners themselves: some are naturally faster, but fast runners also burn more energy even while standing still.
Voltage is how much food they ate that morning. Temperature is the weather.
The race must be fair for every runner in every condition, so organizers plan for the slowest runner on the worst day, and for the fastest, best-fed runner on a hot day too.
Each corner is a straight line on the log axis, with leakage doubling every 15 degrees Celsius (an assumption).

The vertical spread between SS and FF is 25x, and from 25 to 125 degrees Celsius adds another factor of about 100, so the worst-case leakage (FF at 125 degrees Celsius) is tens of thousands of times the best case (SS at -40 degrees Celsius).
Speed varies by tens of percent across the same space. The numbers are illustrative; the shape is the point.
Process variation: tiny manufacturing differences that make no two chips identical. Leakage: current that flows through transistors that should be off.
It grows fast as the chip heats up. Corner: one extreme combination of process, voltage and temperature at which the design is checked.
Guardband: extra margin added so every chip still works at the worst corner. Binning: sorting chips by measured speed and leakage into product grades.
A chip has a 0. 90 volts supply with 3% tolerance. On the low side, that is 27 millivolts less.
Add 20 millivolts lost in the wiring and a 40 millivolts dip when a burst of current is drawn. The transistors then see 0. 90-0. 027-0. 020-0. 040 equals 0.
813 volts, which is 10% low. That costs roughly 11% of the top frequency.
On the temperature side, if leakage doubles every 15 degrees Celsius, then going from 25 degrees Celsius to 85 degrees Celsius multiplies it by 2 to the 4 equals 16 .
That is the whole idea.
"PVT is process, voltage and temperature, the three sources of variation.
Process: die-to-die and within-die differences, where fast silicon has lower thresholds, more drive current and much more leakage.
Voltage: supply tolerance, IR drop and droop; higher voltage is faster but burns V squared dynamic power and more leakage.
Temperature: hot means lower mobility, so usually slower, and exponentially more leakage, with inversion at low voltage.
So we sign off timing and power at the corners and use guardband, binning and adaptive voltage scaling."
